args.title: Network Activity from Two Source IPs: 137.30.122.253 and 137.30.123.234 on Different Dates
args.description: Network traffic analysis reveals activity from TWO distinct source IPs on different dates, not a single coordinated actor as initially described. IP 137.30.122.253 was active on 2004-04-26 from 22:18 to approximately 22:31, performing FTP uploads (port 21) to 137.30.120.40 and HTTP requests (port 80) to google.com and hotmail.com (by17fd.bay17.hotmail.msn.com), as well as IMAP connection (port 143) to 137.30.120.39 lasting ~120 seconds with significant response bytes (462,194 bytes). A DIFFERENT IP address, 137.30.123.234, was active on 2004-04-28 from 21:08 to 21:16, performing HTTP requests to google.com and www.cs.uno.edu with path /~gnome/rhino5.gif. The two IPs represent separate network events, though both relate to the same target network (137.30.x.x range).

args.title: File Named \"contraband.zip\" Uploaded via FTP - Filename Alone Does Not Indicate Prohibited Content
args.description: FTP traffic analysis captured upload of file named \"contraband.zip\" (MIME type application/zip) from 137.30.122.253 to FTP server 137.30.120.40 on 2004-04-26 at 22:26:46 UTC. The file was successfully transferred (FTP reply code 226 \"Transfer complete\"). However, the suspicious filename \"contraband\" is NOT sufficient evidence that the file contains prohibited content. ZIP archives are commonly used for legitimate data compression and backup purposes. Without access to the actual file contents or additional context about what it was intended to contain, the filename alone represents insufficient evidence for classifying this as a security incident. The upload occurred as part of normal FTP activity that also included JPEG image files (rhino1.jpg, rhino3.jpg).

args.title: Username \"gnome\" Appears in FTP Credentials and HTTP Path on Same Server Over Two-Day Period
args.description: Username \"gnome\" appears in two network artifacts that both reference the target server network (137.30.x.x): (1) FTP user credentials used on 2004-04-26 to connect to 137.30.120.40 from IP 137.30.122.253, and (2) HTTP GET request on 2004-04-28 to www.cs.uno.edu (137.30.120.37) accessing path /~gnome/rhino5.gif from IP 137.30.123.234. The gnome username correlation suggests either: (a) the same legitimate user accessing resources from different machines over a two-day period, (b) a legitimate shared account accessed by multiple users, (c) a standard system account that multiple users have access to, or (d) account compromise where credentials were obtained and used subsequently. The two events occurred two days apart from different source IPs, making it unclear whether this represents coordinated malicious activity or routine use of a legitimate account.",severity":"medium","confidence":"confirmed

args.title: Network Artifacts Identified: Multiple Source IPs, Server IPs, and Organizational Domains
args.description: Network analysis identified the following indicators from the captured traffic: Source IPs: 137.30.122.253 (April 26, FTP and HTTP browsing), 137.30.123.234 (April 28, HTTP browsing); FTP server: 137.30.120.40 (receiving file uploads); IMAP server: 137.30.120.39 (email service); HTTP server: 137.30.120.37 (www.cs.uno.edu, University of New Orleans); External servers accessed: google.com, hotmail.msn.com, MSN services; Email address recovered from USB: philg@mit.edu (from copyright string dated 2000); Domains identified: mit.edu (from USB), cs.uno.edu (from HTTP traffic). These artifacts suggest activity involving academic institutions (MIT, University of New Orleans) and normal web/email services. Activity spans April 26-28, 2004 from two separate source IPs on different dates.",severity":"low","confidence":"confirmed"

Bulk extractor analysis of the RHINOUSB.dd USB image recovered email address philg@mit.edu and domain mit.edu from carving of filesystem data. The email address appeared in a copyright string \"copyright 2000 philg@mit.edu\" recovered through data carving, indicating the copyright holder of a file embedded in the USB image. This likely represents MIT-affiliated software or documentation from year 2000 that was stored on the USB drive. The presence of MIT organizational information on the USB suggests connection to Massachusetts Institute of Technology, but the 2000 date indicates this material predates the April 2004 network activity by 4 years.

FTP traffic captured in rhino.pcap shows user \"gnome\" connecting from source IP 137.30.122.253 to FTP server 137.30.120.40 port 21. Between 2004-04-26T22:18:29 and 2004-04-26T22:26:46, the user uploaded four files: rhino1.jpg, rhino3.jpg (uploaded twice), and contraband.zip. All uploads were successful (FTP reply code 226 \"Transfer complete\"). The FTP password was not visible in the captured traffic (shown as hidden by Zeek analysis). The username \"gnome\" represents the account used for FTP authentication. This user account name later appears in an HTTP path (/~gnome/rhino5.gif) on www.cs.uno.edu (137.30.120.37) on 2004-04-28, though accessed from a different source IP (137.30.123.234), suggesting either shared account access or potential account compromise.

What was the actual ownership and permission context of the 'gnome' account on www.cs.uno.edu server?
Was IP 137.30.122.253 an administrative workstation, and what proportion of its traffic was legitimate web browsing vs suspicious?
Does 'contraband.zip' contain actual prohibited content, or is it a legitimate backup/archive with an unfortunate filename?
Was FTP routine for this network/system, or does it represent anomalous behavior?
Are the MIT artifacts on USB from year 2000 legitimate software/documentation, and do they actually connect to recent activity?
Did the USB files (gumbo1.txt, gumbo2.txt) have timestamps consistent with coincidental storage vs active staging?
Does the timeline show a coherent attack progression (initial access → tool deployment → exfiltration), or are events scattered across time?
Could multiple low-confidence artifacts collectively indicate a coordinated operation despite individual explanations?
Does the missing hard drive connect to the network activity, or is it a separate physical security incident?
